subject: rla
title: Text Structure, Author's Purpose, and Point of View
objectives: Students will identify chronological, cause-and-effect, compare-and-contrast, and problem-and-solution structures using signal words and the job of each paragraph.
Students will explain how a sentence or paragraph fits into the overall structure of a text, including passages that open out of time order.
Students will determine an author's purpose for a whole text and for a specific part of it, such as an opening anecdote or a quoted opposing view.
Students will describe an author's point of view using evidence from word choice, included details, and the treatment of opposing views.
Students will identify a narrator's point of view and explain how it shapes what readers know and feel.
teach:
Lesson overview

Week 3 moves learners from what a text says to how and why it says it. Learners will identify the four text structures the GED uses most often (chronological order, cause and effect, compare and contrast, problem and solution), decide an author's purpose for a whole text and for a single part of it, and describe point of view, both the author's position on a subject and the narrator's perspective in a story. These skills appear across every RLA reading passage, and they are also the backbone of Social Studies questions about primary sources and bias.

Objectives

  • Identify chronological, cause-and-effect, compare-and-contrast, and problem-and-solution structures using signal words and the purpose of each paragraph.
  • Explain how a paragraph or section fits into the structure of a whole text.
  • Determine an author's purpose for a whole text and for a specific detail, paragraph, or opening.
  • Describe an author's point of view using evidence such as word choice, what is included, and how opposing views are treated.
  • Identify a narrator's point of view (first person, third person limited, third person omniscient) and explain how it shapes what readers know.

Materials

  • Student Lesson (printed or on screen) and this week's Notes sheet
  • Whiteboard or shared screen; markers in four colors (one per structure)
  • Copies of the warm-up openings, the three worked examples, and the guided-practice passage (all included below)
  • Index cards or a shared document for the exit ticket
  • Week 3 practice items (the standard time passage, items 1–6, are used for independent practice)

60-minute timing plan

SegmentMinutesWhat happens
Warm-up5“What kind of text is this?”: learners classify four short openings
Direct instruction20Text structures and signal words; whole-text vs. part-of-text purpose; author's point of view; narrator's point of view; three worked examples
Guided practice15Whole-group work on the Maple Court passage, five questions
Independent practice15Practice items 1–6 (standard time passage); circulate and coach
Wrap-up5Checks for understanding; exit ticket; assign the week's study plan

Warm-up (5 minutes): What kind of text is this?

Display these four openings. Learners write one word or phrase for each: time order, cause/effect, compare/contrast, or problem/solution, and circle the words that gave it away.

(a) First, unplug the coffee maker and let it cool. Next, fill the tank with equal parts water and vinegar. After the cycle finishes, run two tanks of plain water through it.

(b) Because the Fourth Street bridge closed for repairs, traffic on Main Street doubled. As a result, buses on the Main Street route began running up to fifteen minutes late.

(c) Both apartments are a short walk from the bus line. However, the first one allows pets, while the second one includes parking.

(d) Many parents who work night shifts cannot find child care. One answer is a center that stays open until midnight.

Answers: (a) chronological/sequence (First, Next, After); (b) cause and effect (Because, As a result); (c) compare and contrast (Both, However, while); (d) problem and solution (cannot signals a problem; One answer is signals a solution). Point out that (b) also follows time order. Many texts mix structures; the question is which one organizes the ideas.

Direct instruction (20 minutes)

Talking point 1: What text structure is (2 minutes)

Say: “Text structure is the pattern an author uses to organize ideas. Knowing the pattern is like knowing the floor plan of a house. You can predict where things will be.” Explain that the GED asks about structure in two ways: how a whole passage is organized, and how one paragraph or sentence fits into the whole.

Talking point 2: Four structures and their signal words (6 minutes)

StructureQuestion it answersSignal words
Chronological (time order, sequence)What happened, and in what order? What are the steps?first, next, then, later, finally, before, after, by 1900, in the decades after
Cause and effectWhy did it happen? What did it lead to?because, since, so, as a result, therefore, led to, caused, due to
Compare and contrastHow are two things alike and different?both, similarly, likewise, however, in contrast, unlike, while, on the other hand
Problem and solutionWhat went wrong, and how was it (or could it be) fixed?problem, challenge, difficulty, solution, answer, proposed, solved, one way to

Stress two points. First, signal words are clues, not proof: a passage may use “because” once and still be organized by time. Ask, “What job is each paragraph doing?” Second, a passage can open out of order. Many history articles start with a dramatic moment, then flash back to explain how it happened.

Talking point 3: Author's purpose (4 minutes)

The main purposes are to inform or explain, to persuade, and to entertain (tell a story). On the GED, purpose questions are more specific than “to inform.” Expect choices like “to explain how the railroads created time zones.” Teach learners to ask about parts of a text too: “Why did the author include this anecdote, statistic, quotation, or paragraph here?” Common answers: to hook the reader, to give an example, to show a contrast, to present an opposing view, to provide evidence, or to show the result of something.

Talking point 4: Point of view (4 minutes)

Author's point of view is the author's position or attitude toward the subject. Learners find it with four clues: (1) word choice (“reckless” vs. “bold”), (2) what the author includes or leaves out, (3) how the author treats people who disagree, and (4) the conclusion the author draws. Narrator's point of view applies to stories: first person (“I”; we know only what the narrator knows and believes), third person limited (“she”; we follow one character's thoughts), and third person omniscient (the narrator knows everyone's thoughts). Remind learners that a first-person narrator can be wrong. Readers sometimes understand more than the narrator does.

Talking point 5: Worked examples (4 minutes)

Model each example aloud, thinking through the steps.

Example 1: Cause and effect inside a time-order passage

“In 1990, the town of Pine Hollow had three pharmacies. By 2015, two had closed after a large chain store opened on the highway. Because the remaining pharmacy was across town, older residents without cars began skipping refills. In 2019, the county started a free van that runs from the senior center to the pharmacy twice a week.”

Question: Which relationship does the third sentence show? (a) a comparison of two pharmacies (b) a cause and its effect (c) a step in a process (d) a problem and its solution

Solution. Step 1: Find the signal word: “Because.” Step 2: Identify the parts. Cause: the only pharmacy was across town. Effect: residents without cars skipped refills. Answer: (b). Point out that the paragraph as a whole moves through time (1990, 2015, 2019) and ends with a solution (the van), but the question asks only about one sentence. Choice (d) describes the whole paragraph, not the third sentence.

Example 2: Compare and contrast, point by point

“Electric and gas lawn mowers both cut grass well on a typical yard. Gas mowers, however, run longer and handle thick, tall grass more easily. Electric mowers, on the other hand, are quieter, need no oil changes, and start with the push of a button. For a small yard, the electric model is often the better choice.”

Question: What is the author's purpose, and what is the author's point of view?

Solution. Step 1, structure: “both,” “however,” and “on the other hand” show compare and contrast. Step 2, purpose: the first three sentences inform readers about differences; the last sentence gives a recommendation. So the purpose is to compare the two types and help readers choose. Step 3, point of view: the author is fair to both (gas mowers get real advantages) but favors electric mowers for small yards. A strong answer keeps that limit. “The author thinks gas mowers are bad” distorts the text.

Example 3: Narrator's point of view

“My brother says he is ‘too busy’ to help me move this weekend. Busy doing what, I wonder. When I called Saturday morning, he sounded out of breath, and I heard a hammer in the background. He hung up fast. By Sunday night I had carried every box myself. On Monday, a new bookshelf appeared on my porch, its paint still drying, with a note in his handwriting: ‘For the new place.’”

Question: From what point of view is this told, and how does it affect what readers understand?

Solution. Step 1: The narrator uses “I” and “my,” so it is first person. Step 2: We know only what the narrator knows and feels. The narrator believes the brother is avoiding her. Step 3: The clues she reports (out of breath, a hammer, hanging up fast) let readers guess before she does that he was building a gift. The first-person point of view creates the surprise at the end.

Guided practice (15 minutes)

Read the passage aloud, then work through the questions together. Have learners mark signal words before answering.

Tenants at the Maple Court apartments were shocked when the building's water bill nearly doubled in a single year. The building manager, Ana Ruiz, suspected leaks, but she did not know where to look. She started by asking tenants to report any dripping faucets or toilets that kept running after a flush. Within a month, tenants had reported leaks in 14 of the building's 40 units. Next, Ruiz hired a plumber to repair them and replaced old showerheads with low-flow models. As a result, the following year's water bill fell by almost a third. Ruiz says the most important step was the first one. “The tenants knew where the problems were,” she said. “I just had to ask.”

  1. What structure organizes the whole passage? Expected: problem and solution. The problem is the doubled water bill; the solution is finding and fixing leaks. The steps are told in time order inside the solution.
  2. Name two words or phrases that show sequence. Expected: any two of “started by,” “Within a month,” “Next,” “the following year.”
  3. According to the passage, what caused the water bill to fall? Expected: fixing the leaks in 14 units and installing low-flow showerheads (signal: “As a result”).
  4. What is the author's purpose? Expected: to explain how one building manager solved a costly problem. Accept “to show how asking tenants helped solve the problem.” Do not accept “to persuade landlords to buy low-flow showerheads”; the passage never urges anyone to act.
  5. Why does the author end with Ruiz's quotation? Expected: to emphasize the lesson of the story, that the people affected by a problem can help find it. It gives Ruiz's point of view in her own words.

Independent practice (15 minutes)

Learners complete practice items 1–6 on the standard time passage. Circulate. When a learner is stuck on a structure question, ask, “What job is this paragraph doing: telling what happened next, explaining why, comparing, or describing a problem or fix?” Learners who finish early continue with items 7 and 8 (the career center draft).

Wrap-up (5 minutes)

Checks for understanding

  • “Give me two signal words for compare and contrast.” Expected: any two of both, similarly, however, unlike, in contrast, while, on the other hand.
  • “A passage begins with a crash in 1910 and then explains road conditions in 1890. Is it out of order by mistake?” Expected: No. Authors often open with a dramatic moment to hook readers, then go back to explain causes.
  • “How can you tell an author's point of view if the author never says ‘I think’?” Expected: word choice, what is included or left out, how opponents are treated, and the conclusion.
  • “What can a first-person narrator not tell us?” Expected: other characters' thoughts; the narrator knows only his or her own mind and may misjudge others.

Give the exit ticket from the Post Lesson and assign the study plan.

Common mistakes and how to correct them

Choosing a structure from one signal word. A single “because” does not make a whole passage cause and effect. Correction: have learners label the job of each paragraph in the margin, then decide.

Mixing up a part and the whole. Learners answer a question about one paragraph with the structure of the whole passage (or the reverse). Correction: underline the scope words in the question: “paragraph 3,” “the passage,” “the first sentence.”

Vague purpose answers. “To inform” is almost never enough. Correction: require the “to ___ readers about ___” frame, then match it to the most specific choice.

Confusing the author with the people quoted. An author who reports critics' complaints is not necessarily agreeing with them. Correction: ask, “Whose words are these? Does the author accept or answer them?”

Trusting a first-person narrator completely. Correction: ask learners to list what the narrator believes and what the details actually show.

Differentiation

Support: Give a color-coded signal word card (one color per structure). Let learners work with one paragraph at a time and name its job before looking at the whole passage. Read the guided-practice passage aloud twice. Provide the sentence frame “The author wrote this to ___ readers about ___.”

Stretch: Ask learners to rewrite the Maple Court passage as a compare-and-contrast text (the building before and after the repairs) and discuss what changes. Have them rewrite Example 3 in third person omniscient and explain why the ending loses its surprise. Ask them to find a news article and describe the author's point of view using two specific word choices as evidence.

Teacher note: On the GED, point of view in informational texts often overlaps with bias. Save the full discussion of bias for the Social Studies practices week, but introduce the idea here: a point of view is not wrong just because it is one-sided. Learners should describe it accurately before judging it.

How this shows up on the GED

Structure, purpose, and point of view questions appear with both informational and literary passages. Expect wording such as:

  • “How does the author organize the information in paragraphs 2 through 4?”
  • “Which statement best describes the relationship between paragraph 3 and paragraph 4?”
  • “Why does the author begin the passage with …?” or “What is the purpose of paragraph 5?”
  • “Which statement best describes the author's point of view toward …?”
  • “How does the narrator's point of view affect the reader's understanding of …?”
  • Drag-and-drop items that put events in time order or sort details into cause and effect.
  • Hot spot items that ask learners to click the sentence that states a problem, a cause, or the author's position.
  • Editing (drop-down) items that ask for the transition that best fits the relationship between two sentences, such as however, as a result, or for example.

The extended response also depends on this week: to judge which of two arguments is better supported, learners must first describe each author's position and purpose accurately.
student:
Why this skill matters

Good readers do not just ask, “What does this say?” They also ask, “How is this put together, and why did the author write it this way?” On the GED Reasoning Through Language Arts test, many questions ask how a passage is organized, why the author included a certain part, or what the author or narrator thinks. This week you will learn to answer those questions quickly and with evidence.

Four common text structures

Text structure is the pattern an author uses to organize ideas. Most GED passages use one or more of these four patterns.

StructureWhat it doesSignal words
Chronological (time order or sequence)Tells events or steps in the order they happenfirst, next, then, later, finally, before, after, in 1920
Cause and effectExplains why something happened or what it led tobecause, since, so, as a result, therefore, led to, due to
Compare and contrastShows how two or more things are alike and differentboth, similarly, likewise, however, unlike, in contrast, while
Problem and solutionDescribes a problem and one or more ways to fix itproblem, challenge, solution, answer, proposed, solved

Key idea: Signal words are clues, not proof. To find the structure, ask what job each paragraph is doing: telling what happened next, explaining why, comparing, or describing a problem or a fix.

How to identify the structure

  1. Read the question and note its scope: one sentence, one paragraph, or the whole passage.
  2. Circle the signal words in that part of the text.
  3. In a few words, write the job of each paragraph (for example, “the problem,” “first attempt to fix it,” “result”).
  4. Choose the structure that fits all of the paragraphs in the question's scope.

Watch for passages that start out of order. Many articles open with a dramatic moment and then go back in time to explain how it happened. The passage is still mainly chronological after that opening.

Author's purpose

An author writes to inform or explain, to persuade, or to entertain (tell a story). GED answer choices are more specific, so finish this sentence: “The author wrote this to ___ readers about ___.”

You will also be asked why an author included one part of a text. Common reasons:

  • to catch the reader's interest (a story, question, or surprising fact at the start)
  • to give an example or evidence for a claim
  • to show a contrast or a change
  • to present an opposing view, often so the author can answer it
  • to show the result or importance of something

Point of view

Author's point of view is the author's position or attitude toward a subject. Authors do not always say “I think,” so look for these clues:

  • Word choice: “a reckless plan” and “a bold plan” describe the same plan in very different ways.
  • What is included or left out: does the author give only one side's evidence?
  • How others are treated: are opposing views reported fairly, mocked, or ignored?
  • The conclusion: where does the author end up?

Narrator's point of view is the perspective a story is told from.

Point of viewClueWhat readers learn
First personThe narrator says “I” and “we”Only what the narrator sees, thinks, and believes. The narrator can be mistaken.
Third person limited“He” or “she”; one character's thoughtsOne character's inner life; others are seen from outside.
Third person omniscient“He,” “she,” “they”; many characters' thoughtsWhat everyone thinks and feels.

Worked examples

Example 1: Find the structure

“For years, the Westfield Community Center had no way to reach families who did not use the internet. Flyers posted on the center's door reached only people who already visited. Last fall, the center began mailing a one-page newsletter to every home in the neighborhood. Attendance at its free tax-help nights rose from 30 people to 85.”

Step 1. Job of each sentence: the problem (no way to reach families), why flyers failed, the fix (a mailed newsletter), the result (attendance rose).

Step 2. The pattern is problem and solution. The last sentence shows the effect of the solution.

Example 2: Purpose of a part

“Some people say public pools cost too much to run. It is true that pools are expensive to staff and heat. But a single summer of free swim lessons can prevent drownings, and no budget line is worth more than a child's life.”

Question: Why does the author include the first two sentences?

Step 1. Whose idea is in sentence 1? People who oppose pools, not the author.

Step 2. The word “But” shows the author turning to answer them.

Answer: to present an opposing view so the author can respond to it. The author's own point of view is that pools are worth the cost.

Example 3: Narrator's point of view

“I could tell the new manager did not like me. She kept asking how I organized the stockroom and wrote down everything I said. On Friday, she called a staff meeting. ‘Starting Monday,’ she announced, ‘every store in the district will use Mario's stockroom system.’”

Step 1. “I” shows first person. The narrator is Mario.

Step 2. Mario believes the manager dislikes him. The details (asking questions, taking notes, adopting his system) show she admired his work.

Step 3. Because we see only Mario's thoughts, we share his worry until the surprise at the end.

Strategy: For any “why did the author include” question, look at what comes right before and right after that part. Its purpose usually depends on its neighbors.

Try it

1. “Unlike city buses, which stop every few blocks, express buses stop only at major stations. Both cost the same to ride, but express buses can cut a long commute by twenty minutes.” What structure is used? Name two signal words.

Show answer

Compare and contrast. Signal words: “Unlike,” “Both,” and “but.” Any two are correct.

2. “Heavy rain soaked the fields for three weeks in May. Farmers could not plant on time, so the corn harvest was smaller than usual. Prices for corn rose by fall.” Name one cause and one effect.

Show answer

Cause: weeks of heavy rain (farmers could not plant on time). Effects: a smaller corn harvest and higher corn prices. Any correct cause-and-effect pair is acceptable, such as “smaller harvest” causing “higher prices.”

3. An article about a new library begins: “At 9:00 a.m. on opening day, the line of people waiting to get in stretched around the block.” Why might the author start this way?

Show answer

To catch the reader's interest and show right away how popular or needed the library is. The rest of the article can then explain how it came to be.

4. “The so-called ‘improvement’ plan will tear up a beloved park to build yet another parking garage.” What is the author's point of view, and which words show it?

Show answer

The author opposes the plan. Clues: “so-called” and the quotation marks around “improvement” suggest it is not really an improvement; “tear up” and “beloved” are emotional; “yet another” suggests there are too many garages already.

5. “Lena watched her grandfather fold the flag and wondered what he was thinking. He was thinking about the letter in the drawer. He had no idea that she had already read it.” Is this first person, third person limited, or third person omniscient? Explain.

Show answer

Third person omniscient. The narrator uses “she” and “he,” not “I,” so it is third person. The narrator tells us what Lena wonders and what her grandfather is thinking, so the narrator knows more than one character’s mind. That makes it omniscient, not limited.
post:
Summary of key points

  • Text structure is how an author organizes ideas. The four most common structures are chronological (time order), cause and effect, compare and contrast, and problem and solution.
  • Signal words are clues, but always check the job of each paragraph. Many passages mix structures, and some open out of order with a dramatic moment.
  • Author's purpose is the reason for writing: to inform or explain, to persuade, or to entertain. Make it specific: “to ___ readers about ___.”
  • Ask why an author included a part: to hook the reader, give evidence, show a contrast, present an opposing view, or show a result.
  • Author's point of view is the author's position, shown through word choice, what is included, how others are treated, and the conclusion.
  • Narrator's point of view can be first person, third person limited, or third person omniscient. A first-person narrator may not understand everything.

Exit ticket

1. Which structure uses the signal words as a result and due to?

Show answer

Cause and effect.

2. A passage describes a town's flooding problem, then two ways the town tried to stop it. What structure is this?

Show answer

Problem and solution.

3. Why is “to inform” usually a weak answer to a purpose question?

Show answer

It is too general. GED choices name what the author informs readers about and often why, so you need the most specific accurate choice.

4. An author quotes a critic of a new law. Does that mean the author agrees with the critic? How can you tell?

Show answer

Not necessarily. Check whether the author answers the critic (often after a word like but or however), what the author concludes, and the author's own word choices.

5. What is one thing a first-person narrator cannot tell readers directly?

Show answer

What other characters are thinking. The narrator knows only his or her own thoughts and may misjudge others.

Reflection

  • Which structure was easiest for you to spot, and which was hardest? Why?
  • Think of a news story or social media post you read recently. What was the author's purpose, and what was the author's point of view? How could you tell?
  • When you tell a story about your own day, you are a first-person narrator. What might a listener not learn from your version?

This week's study plan

DayWhat to doTime
Day 1Reread the Student Lesson. Redo the Try it problems without looking at the answers. Make a signal word card for the four structures.25 min
Day 2Study the vocabulary. Read one news article and label the job of each paragraph in the margin. Name its overall structure.25 min
Day 3Complete practice items 1–6. Read every explanation, even for items you got right.30 min
Day 4Complete practice items 7–12. For each miss, write whether you confused the part with the whole, trusted a signal word too much, or mixed up the author with someone quoted.30 min
Day 5Point of view drill: find two short texts on the same topic (for example, a company announcement and a customer review). Write one sentence describing each author's point of view, with two word choices as evidence.25 min
Day 6Take this week's Practice GED for Reasoning Through Language Arts under timed conditions.40 min, continue on Day 7 if needed
Day 7Finish the Practice GED if needed. Review every missed question and list the skills to work on.30 min

Test-taking strategy: Label the paragraphs

Before answering structure or purpose questions, spend about thirty seconds writing a two- to four-word label for each paragraph on your scratch paper: “hook: 1883,” “problem: many times,” “solution: zones,” “critics,” “law: 1918.” Your labels become a map of the passage. Most structure and purpose questions can then be answered by reading your map instead of rereading the whole text.

vocab.def: The pattern an author uses to organize ideas in a text.
vocab.example: A history article that tells events in the order they happened uses chronological structure.

vocab.def: Organizing events or steps in the order they happen in time. Also called time order or sequence.
vocab.example: First the dough rises; then it is shaped; finally it is baked.

vocab.def: A structure that explains why something happened (the cause) and what happened as a result (the effect).
vocab.example: Because the road flooded, the school canceled classes.

vocab.def: A structure that shows how two or more things are alike (compare) and different (contrast).
vocab.example: Both jobs pay weekly; however, only one offers health insurance.

vocab.def: A structure that describes a problem and one or more ways it was or could be solved.
vocab.example: Long lines at the clinic were cut in half when it began taking appointments online.

vocab.def: Words or phrases that show how ideas are connected. Also called transitions.
vocab.example: As a result signals an effect; in contrast signals a difference.

vocab.def: The reason an author writes a text or includes a part of it: to inform or explain, to persuade, or to entertain.
vocab.example: A safety guide is written to explain how to use a ladder correctly.

vocab.def: A short story about a real event, often used to open a text and catch the reader's interest.
vocab.example: An article on job training begins with one worker's first day in a new career.

vocab.def: The author's position or attitude toward a subject, shown through word choice, what is included, and the conclusion.
vocab.example: Calling a plan “wasteful” shows the author opposes it.

vocab.def: A position that disagrees with the author's. Authors often present it and then answer it.
vocab.example: “Some say the fee is too high. However, …”

vocab.def: The voice that tells a story. The narrator may or may not be a character in it.
vocab.example: In a story that begins “I never meant to leave home,” the narrator is a character.

vocab.def: A story told by a narrator who is a character and uses “I” or “we.” Readers know only what that narrator knows.
vocab.example: “I thought the call was bad news, so I let it ring.”

vocab.def: A story told with “he,” “she,” or “they” that shares the thoughts of only one character.
vocab.example: “Marcus wondered whether his sister was still angry.”

vocab.def: A story told by an all-knowing narrator who shares the thoughts of many characters.
vocab.example: “Marcus wondered whether his sister was still angry. She had already forgotten the argument.”

Week 3 RLA Study Sheet: Text Structure, Author's Purpose, Point of View

Text structures

StructureJobSignal words
ChronologicalEvents or steps in orderfirst, next, then, later, finally, before, after, dates
Cause and effectWhy it happened; what it led tobecause, since, so, as a result, therefore, led to, due to
Compare and contrastAlike and differentboth, similarly, however, unlike, in contrast, while, on the other hand
Problem and solutionWhat went wrong; how to fix itproblem, challenge, solution, answer, proposed, solved

Finding the structure

  1. Note the scope: sentence, paragraph, or passage.
  2. Circle signal words.
  3. Label each paragraph's job.
  4. Pick the structure that fits all of them.

Author's purpose

  • Inform/explain, persuade, entertain
  • Frame: “to ___ readers about ___”
  • Purpose of a part: hook, example/evidence, contrast, opposing view, result

Author's point of view clues

  • Word choice (reckless vs. bold)
  • What is included or left out
  • How opponents are treated
  • The conclusion

Narrator's point of view

  • First person: “I”; only the narrator's mind; may be mistaken
  • Third limited: “he/she”; one character's thoughts
  • Third omniscient: many characters' thoughts

Key idea: Signal words are clues, not proof. Ask what job each paragraph is doing.

Strategy: Label each paragraph in two to four words before answering. Look before and after a part to find its purpose.

Common mistakes: choosing a structure from one signal word; answering about the whole passage when asked about one part; picking a vague purpose; assuming the author agrees with everyone quoted; trusting a first-person narrator completely.

stimuli.title: Setting the Nation's Clocks
stimuli.source: Original passage written for KCE GED Prep.
stimuli.html:
[1] On November 18, 1883, people in many American towns lived through what is sometimes called “the day of two noons.” In city after city, when the clocks reached twelve, railroad workers and jewelers stopped them, waited several minutes, and started them again, or turned the hands back so that noon arrived a second time. Nothing about the sun had changed. What had changed was the way the country agreed to tell time.

[2] Before that day, most towns kept their own local time. Noon was the moment the sun stood highest in the sky over that particular town. Because the sun appears to move from east to west, noon arrived a little later with every mile a traveler went west. When it was noon in one town, it might be a few minutes past noon in a town to the east and a few minutes before noon in a town to the west. For people who rarely traveled more than a few miles from home, these small differences hardly mattered.

[3] The railroads changed that. As train lines stretched across the country in the decades after the Civil War, local time became a serious problem. Each railroad set its schedules by the time in its home city or at its major stations, so a single station might display several clocks, each showing a different railroad's time. By the early 1880s, railroads in the United States were using dozens of different time standards. Travelers missed connections because they misread schedules. Worse, when two trains shared a single track, a difference of even a few minutes between the crews' watches could lead to a deadly collision.

[4] Several people proposed solutions. Around 1870, a New York school principal named Charles Dowd suggested dividing the country into bands, or zones, each one hour apart, with every clock inside a zone showing the same time. In the end, the railroads acted on their own rather than waiting for the government. A railroad official named William F. Allen drew up a plan that placed the nation's rail lines into four main time zones. The railroads agreed to switch to the new system at noon on November 18, 1883. That decision produced the day of two noons.

[5] Not everyone welcomed the change. Some town leaders and newspaper writers complained that private companies had no right to decide what time it was. Critics described sun time as natural and honest, and they mocked the new system as “railroad time.” A number of towns kept their local time for years. Over time, however, as more businesses, schools, and courts followed the railroad schedules, standard time became the time most people actually lived by.

[6] Congress finally made the system official in 1918, when it passed the Standard Time Act. The law gave a federal agency the power to set the boundaries of the time zones, and the same law created daylight saving time for the first time in the nation's history. Today, most people never stop to think that their clocks show the same time as clocks hundreds of miles away. That agreement, which seems so natural now, began as a practical answer to a dangerous problem on the rails.

stimuli.title: The Torque Wrench
stimuli.source: Original fiction written for KCE GED Prep.
stimuli.html:
[1] Walt Brenner had not said more than ten words to me in my first two weeks at Delgado's Garage, and six of them were “Do it again. Do it again.”

[2] He said it on my first Monday, when I rotated the tires on a delivery van and he walked over, crouched by the front wheel, and ran his thumb across each lug nut as if he were reading Braille. He said it again on Thursday, after I changed the oil in a pickup and left a smear of grease on the fender. I wiped the fender. He did not say thank you.

[3] “He's like that with everybody,” said Marisol, who ran the front counter and had worked there longer than anyone except Walt. I did not believe her. I had watched him joke with the parts delivery driver and lend his good flashlight to Kenny, the other new hire, who once dropped a socket wrench into an engine and spent an hour fishing it out. Nobody told Kenny to do it again.

[4] By the end of the second week, I had decided that Walt simply did not think I belonged under a car, or maybe that a woman did not, and I had started rehearsing what I would say to Mr. Delgado when I quit.

[5] On Friday I did a brake job on a minivan that belonged to a woman with three car seats in the back. I took my time. I checked every bolt with the torque wrench, twice, and wrote the numbers on the work order the way Walt did, in small square print. When I rolled out from under the van, Walt was standing there reading my numbers. He picked up the wrench, checked one wheel himself, and set the wrench down on the bench.

[6] “Okay,” he said, and walked away.

[7] I was so angry I almost missed what happened next. Walt went into the office, and through the open door I saw him take the clipboard with next month's schedule off its nail. He crossed something out and wrote above it. Then he hung the clipboard back up and went to lunch.

[8] When he was gone, I looked. Every Saturday in March had said “Brakes and alignment: W. Brenner.” Now, on the last two Saturdays, his name had a line through it. Above it, in that small square print, was mine.

[9] Kenny's name was not on the schedule at all.

stimuli.title: Draft Newsletter Article: Two Paths into the Trades
stimuli.source: Original document written for KCE GED Prep.
stimuli.html:
Eastside Career Center Monthly Newsletter
Draft article (for review)

(1) Many adults who want a career in the skilled trades face the same question: should they enroll in a certificate program at a community college, or should they look for an apprenticeship? Both paths can lead to steady, well-paying work as an electrician, plumber, welder, or heating and cooling technician. The two paths differ, however, in how people learn, how they pay, and how long they train.

(2) A certificate program teaches students mainly in classrooms and campus workshops. Many programs last one year or less, so graduates can begin looking for jobs quickly. (A) certificate students do not have a job waiting for them; they must find an employer on their own after they finish. They also usually pay tuition, although many qualify for financial aid.

(3) An apprenticeship works differently. Apprentices are hired by an employer or a union from the start, and they learn mostly on the job under an experienced worker, with some classroom hours added. (B) they earn a paycheck while they train, apprentices usually do not take on student debt. Apprenticeships take longer to complete, however, often three to five years, and openings can be hard to get.

(4) Which path is right depends on the person. (C) someone who needs to finish training within a year may prefer a certificate, while someone who needs to earn money during training may prefer an apprenticeship. Our career counselors can help you weigh your choices. Call the front desk to schedule a free appointment.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes how paragraphs 3 and 4 are organized?
options: Paragraph 3 describes a problem created by local time on the railroads, and paragraph 4 explains how people proposed and adopted a solution.
Paragraph 3 compares sun time with railroad time, and paragraph 4 explains why most people preferred sun time.
Paragraphs 3 and 4 list, step by step, how a railroad station sets its clocks each day.
Paragraphs 3 and 4 present the views of critics who opposed the new time zones.
items.hint: What goes wrong in paragraph 3? What do people do about it in paragraph 4?
items.explain:
Step 1. Label paragraph 3. It says local time “became a serious problem” and lists what went wrong: many clocks at one station, missed connections, and possible collisions. Its job: the problem.

Step 2. Label paragraph 4. It opens with “Several people proposed solutions” and describes Dowd's idea and Allen's plan, which the railroads adopted. Its job: the solution.

Step 3. Together, the paragraphs follow a problem and solution structure. Correct.

The sun time choice is wrong because neither paragraph says people preferred sun time. The step-by-step choice describes a process the passage never explains. The critics choice describes paragraph 5, not paragraphs 3 and 4.

items.prompt: What is the author's main purpose in this passage?
options: to explain how and why the United States came to use standard time zones
to persuade readers that the country should return to local sun time
to entertain readers with a story about a railroad crash in 1883
to instruct readers on how to set a clock to the correct time zone
items.hint: Use the frame “The author wrote this to ___ readers about ___.” Does the author ever ask readers to do or believe something?
items.explain:
Step 1. Look at what each paragraph does: it describes the switch in 1883, explains local time, explains the problems the railroads faced, describes the solution, reports the critics, and tells how the system became law in 1918.

Step 2. All of this explains a piece of history: how standard time began and why. The author never urges readers to act. The correct choice is the one about explaining how and why the country came to use standard time zones.

Step 3. Check the distractors. The passage does not argue for a return to sun time; the critics' views are reported, not adopted, and the conclusion calls standard time “a practical answer.” No specific crash is described; paragraph 3 says only that a time difference “could lead to” a collision. The passage gives no instructions for setting a clock.

items.prompt: Click the sentence from paragraph 3 that states the problem that the rest of the paragraph explains.
spans: As train lines stretched across the country in the decades after the Civil War, local time became a serious problem.
Each railroad set its schedules by the time in its home city or at its major stations, so a single station might display several clocks, each showing a different railroad's time.
By the early 1880s, railroads in the United States were using dozens of different time standards.
Travelers missed connections because they misread schedules.
Worse, when two trains shared a single track, a difference of even a few minutes between the crews' watches could lead to a deadly collision.
items.hint: One sentence uses the word “problem.” Do the other sentences give details about it?
items.explain:
Step 1. Look for the sentence that names the problem in general terms: “As train lines stretched across the country…, local time became a serious problem.” Correct.

Step 2. Check that the other sentences explain it. Several clocks at one station, dozens of time standards, missed connections, and possible collisions are all details showing why local time was a problem.

Step 3. Check the trap. “The railroads changed that” is a transition. It links back to paragraph 2 but does not say what the problem was. The collision sentence is the most dramatic, but it is only one example of the problem.

items.prompt: The passage does not tell events in the order they happened. Put these events in the order in which they actually occurred. Drag each event to its position.
choices: Congress passes the Standard Time Act.
Charles Dowd suggests dividing the country into time zones one hour apart.
Before the railroads spread across the country, towns set their clocks by the sun, and few people notice the small differences.
The railroads switch to four main time zones, creating the day of two noons.
items.hint: Paragraph 1 is a hook. Find a date or time clue for each event: “Before that day,” “Around 1870,” 1883, and 1918.
items.explain:
Step 1. Find a time clue for each event.

  • Towns keep sun time and few people notice: paragraph 2 describes local time, and paragraph 3 says “The railroads changed that” in the decades after the Civil War, so this came before the railroads spread. 1st.
  • Dowd's suggestion: “Around 1870” (paragraph 4), more than a decade before 1883. 2nd.
  • The railroads switch: November 18, 1883 (paragraphs 1 and 4). 3rd.
  • The Standard Time Act: 1918 (paragraph 6). 4th.

Step 2. Notice the trap. The passage opens with the day of two noons, so a reader who follows the order of the passage might place 1883 first. The author starts with that event to hook the reader, then goes back in time.

items.prompt: Why does the author begin the passage by describing “the day of two noons” instead of beginning with how towns kept local time?
options: to catch the reader's interest with a surprising event and then explain the history that led to it
to show that the change to standard time happened slowly over many years
to argue that the railroads created confusion by changing the nation's clocks
to prove that local sun time was more accurate than railroad time
items.hint: Think about how a strange or surprising scene affects a reader. What does paragraph 2 do right after it?
items.explain:
Step 1. Notice the structure. Paragraph 1 describes a strange moment in 1883. Paragraph 2 then begins “Before that day” and goes back in time.

Step 2. Opening with an unusual event (clocks striking noon twice) makes readers curious. The rest of the passage answers the question it raises: why did that happen? The correct choice is the one about catching the reader's interest with a surprising event before explaining the history.

Step 3. Check the distractors. The day of two noons was a single day, so it does not show a slow change. The author says the change solved “a dangerous problem,” so the author is not arguing that it created confusion; the confusion came from the earlier system. The passage never claims sun time was more accurate.

items.prompt: According to paragraph 3, what was one effect of each railroad setting its schedules by the time in its own home city or major stations?
options: A single station might display several clocks showing different times.
Congress quickly passed a law requiring every town to use standard time.
Towns across the country stopped keeping their own local time.
Railroads began building separate tracks so that trains would never share a line.
items.hint: Find the signal word “so” in paragraph 3. What comes right after it?
items.explain:
Step 1. Find the cause in paragraph 3: “Each railroad set its schedules by the time in its home city or at its major stations.”

Step 2. The signal word so introduces the effect: “a single station might display several clocks, each showing a different railroad's time.” The correct choice is the one about a single station displaying several clocks.

Step 3. Check the distractors. Congress did not act until 1918, decades later, and not “quickly.” Towns did not stop keeping local time because of this; in fact, paragraph 5 says many kept local time for years even after 1883. The passage never mentions building separate tracks.

items.prompt:
Read the draft newsletter article. Then choose the transition that best completes each blank in these excerpts.

Paragraph 2, blank (A): Many programs last one year or less, so graduates can begin looking for jobs quickly. {{0}} certificate students do not have a job waiting for them; they must find an employer on their own after they finish.

Paragraph 3, blank (B): {{1}} they earn a paycheck while they train, apprentices usually do not take on student debt.

Paragraph 4, blank (C): Which path is right depends on the person. {{2}} someone who needs to finish training within a year may prefer a certificate, while someone who needs to earn money during training may prefer an apprenticeship.

options: However,
As a result,
Similarly,
For instance,
Because
Although
Unless
Until
For example,
In contrast,
Otherwise,
Meanwhile,

items.hint: Decide how each sentence relates to the one before it: a contrast, a cause, or an example. Then pick the transition that signals that relationship.
items.explain:
Blank (A). Step 1: The sentence before gives an advantage (graduates can look for jobs quickly). Step 2: The next sentence gives a drawback (no job is waiting). An advantage followed by a drawback is a contrast. Step 3: “However,” signals contrast. Correct. “As a result” wrongly says a short program causes students to lack a job. “Similarly” signals a likeness, and “For instance” signals an example; neither fits.

Blank (B). Step 1: Earning a paycheck is the reason apprentices avoid debt, so the relationship is cause and effect. Step 2: “Because” introduces a cause. Correct. “Although” signals an unexpected contrast, which makes no sense here. “Unless” and “Until” change the meaning to a condition or a time limit that the paragraph does not state.

Blank (C). Step 1: The first sentence makes a general point (the right path depends on the person). Step 2: The next sentence gives two specific people as illustrations. Step 3: “For example,” introduces an illustration. Correct. “In contrast” is wrong because the sentence does not differ from the one before it; it explains it. “Otherwise” and “Meanwhile” signal a condition and a time relationship that are not present.

items.prompt: How does the writer organize paragraphs 2 and 3 of the draft article?
options: by describing one training path in paragraph 2 and the other in paragraph 3 so that readers can compare the two
by listing, in time order, the steps a person must follow to become a licensed electrician
by describing a shortage of skilled workers in paragraph 2 and a solution to it in paragraph 3
by explaining the causes of student debt in paragraph 2 and its effects in paragraph 3
items.hint: Paragraph 1 promises to explain how the two paths “differ.” What does each of the next two paragraphs describe?
items.explain:
Step 1. Label each paragraph. Paragraph 2 describes certificate programs: where students learn, how long it takes, finding a job, and tuition. Paragraph 3 describes apprenticeships on the same points: where apprentices learn, pay and debt, length, and openings.

Step 2. Paragraph 1 says the two paths “differ” in how people learn, pay, and train, and paragraph 3 opens with “An apprenticeship works differently.” These are compare-and-contrast signals. The correct choice is the one about describing one path in paragraph 2 and the other in paragraph 3 so readers can compare them. (This is sometimes called a block comparison: one subject per paragraph.)

Step 3. Check the distractors. The article never gives steps for becoming an electrician. It never describes a worker shortage. Student debt is mentioned only once, in paragraph 3, so it is not the organizing idea of both paragraphs.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes the point of view from which the story is told?
options: It is told in the first person by a new mechanic who shares her own thoughts but can only guess what Walt is thinking.
It is told in the third person by a narrator who reveals the thoughts of Walt, Marisol, and the new mechanic.
It is told in the first person by Walt, who explains why he is strict with new employees.
It is told in the third person by Marisol, who watches the other workers from the front counter.
items.hint: Who says “I” in the story? Does the story ever tell us directly what Walt is thinking?
items.explain:
Step 1. The narrator uses “I” and “me” (“ten words to me,” “I rotated the tires”), so the story is in the first person.

Step 2. Identify the narrator. The “I” is a new worker in her first two weeks at the garage. She is not Walt, because she describes Walt from the outside, and not Marisol, because Marisol speaks to her.

Step 3. Ask what the narrator can know. She tells her own feelings (“I was so angry”) but never Walt's thoughts; she can only observe what he does. The correct choice is the one about a new mechanic who shares her own thoughts but can only guess what Walt is thinking.

The third-person choices are wrong because the narrator says “I.” The Walt choice is wrong because Walt never explains himself; he barely speaks.

items.prompt: The narrator believes that Walt does not think she belongs at the garage. Which two details suggest that Walt actually trusts her work? Select two answers.
options: Walt crosses his own name off the March schedule for brakes and alignment and writes hers above it.
Kenny's name does not appear on the schedule at all.
Walt lends his good flashlight to Kenny.
Marisol says that Walt is “like that with everybody.”
Walt does not say thank you after the narrator wipes the grease off the fender.
items.hint: Look for what Walt does at the end of the story, after he checks her brake job. Which details compare her to the other new hire in a way that favors her?
items.explain:
Step 1. Focus on actions that show trust, not friendliness. Trust at a garage means being given important work.

Step 2. Walt replaces his own name with the narrator's for brake and alignment work, which is safety work, right after checking her careful brake job. This shows he trusts her with his own jobs. Correct.

Step 3. The final line, “Kenny's name was not on the schedule at all,” contrasts her with the other new hire. Walt was friendlier to Kenny, but he chose the narrator, not Kenny, for the work. Correct.

Step 4. Check the distractors. Lending the flashlight shows friendliness to Kenny, not trust in the narrator. Marisol's comment suggests Walt's strictness is not personal, but it does not show that he trusts the narrator's work. Not saying thank you is part of the narrator's evidence that Walt dislikes her.

items.skill: Effect of narrator's point of view
items.prompt: How does the first-person point of view affect the reader's experience of the story?
options: Because readers know only what the narrator thinks, they share her belief that Walt dislikes her until his actions at the end reveal a different view of her.
Because the narrator explains Walt's thoughts throughout, readers know from the start that he plans to give her his Saturday shifts.
Because the narrator is angry, readers cannot trust any of the events she describes, including the change to the schedule.
Because the story is told by Marisol, readers learn how everyone at the garage feels about the new employees.
items.hint: What does the narrator believe for most of the story? When do readers learn something that changes that belief?
items.explain:
Step 1. In first person, readers see only the narrator's thoughts. For most of the story, she believes Walt does not think she belongs (paragraph 4) and plans to quit.

Step 2. Walt's thoughts are never shown. Readers learn his real opinion only through an action at the end: he gives her his brake and alignment shifts.

Step 3. So the point of view creates a surprise and shows the gap between what the narrator believes and what is true. The correct choice is the one about readers sharing the narrator's belief that Walt dislikes her until his actions at the end reveal a different view.

The choice saying the narrator explains Walt's thoughts throughout is wrong because the narrator never explains Walt's thoughts. The choice saying readers cannot trust any of the events goes too far: an angry narrator may misjudge people, but she reports actions such as the schedule change directly, and nothing in the story suggests those events are false. The choice naming Marisol as the storyteller is wrong because Marisol is not the narrator.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes the author's point of view toward the adoption of standard time?
options: The author sees standard time as a sensible solution to a real problem and reports the critics' complaints without agreeing with them.
The author agrees with the critics that private companies should not have been allowed to decide what time it was.
The author believes that Congress, not the railroads, should have created the time zones in 1883.
The author thinks standard time was unnecessary because the differences between towns were only a few minutes.
items.hint: Reread the last sentence of the passage. What words does the author use to describe standard time in their own voice?
items.explain:
Step 1. Find the author's own words, not the critics'. The conclusion calls standard time “a practical answer to a dangerous problem on the rails” and says the agreement “seems so natural now.” Paragraph 3 calls local time “a serious problem.” These word choices show the author views standard time favorably.

Step 2. Look at how the critics are treated. Paragraph 5 reports their complaints (“Critics described…”), then turns with “however” to explain that standard time won out. The author reports the objection but does not adopt it. The correct choice is the one saying the author sees standard time as a sensible solution and reports the critics' complaints without agreeing with them.

Step 3. Check the distractors. The choice saying the author agrees with the critics confuses the critics' view with the author's. The choice about Congress acting in 1883 is not stated; the author says the railroads acted “rather than waiting for the government” but never says the government should have acted first. The choice calling standard time unnecessary distorts paragraph 2: the small differences “hardly mattered” only for people who did not travel far, and paragraph 3 explains that they became dangerous for the railroads.
